questions.q: Which distribution style copies an entire table onto every compute node?
options: ALL
EVEN
KEY
SORTKEY
questions.explain: DISTSTYLE ALL is reserved for small, frequently-joined dimension tables where a full copy on every node is cheap and guarantees local joins.

questions.q: Why does a shared DISTKEY on a join column between two tables improve join performance?
options: Rows with matching key values land on the same slice, so the join happens locally without shuffling data across the network
It automatically converts the join into a cross join
It removes the need for a leader node
It compresses the join columns more than other columns
questions.explain: KEY distribution hashes rows by the DISTKEY, so colocating both tables on that column lets matching rows join without network shuffling.

questions.q: What happens when you choose a low-cardinality column (e.g. a 3-value status field) as a DISTKEY?
options: Data skew — rows pile onto only a few slices, and the query slows to the pace of the most overloaded slice
Redshift automatically switches the table to DISTSTYLE ALL
Nothing — cardinality has no effect on distribution
The load fails immediately with an error
questions.explain: A low-cardinality DISTKEY produces few distinct hash buckets, so rows concentrate on a handful of slices, creating a bottleneck the whole MPP query waits on.

questions.q: What is a zone map used for?
options: Storing the min/max value range for each block, so queries can skip blocks that can't match a filter
Mapping which AWS Availability Zone each compute node runs in
Tracking which IAM roles can query a table
Recording the DISTSTYLE of every table in the cluster
questions.explain: Zone maps let Redshift skip reading blocks whose stored min/max range proves they can't contain a row matching the query's filter.

options: The physical order rows are stored in on disk within each slice
Which compute node a row is distributed to
The IAM role used to load a table
Whether a table uses columnar or row storage
questions.explain: SORTKEY orders rows physically on disk (e.g. by date), which is what makes zone-map block skipping effective for range filters.
